newsitem.title: UK: Saudi sees no change as OPEC aims not to make waves.
newsitem.headline: Saudi sees no change as OPEC aims not to make waves.

text.p: OPEC ministers meeting in 10 days time will want to avoid sending any unexpected waves over the bows of vulnerable world oil markets, OPEC delegates and insiders said this week.
But the recent slump in world crude prices is likely to put some bite back into quarrels over OPEC's leaky quota system.
"We don't see any need for big changes," said a Gulf source familiar with Saudi oil policy. "It should be low profile. That is best."

He indicated that the Gulf kingdom was most likely to go along with a number of Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) members who have already said they wanted to keep crude production quotas unchanged for the second half of the year.
Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil exporter, would keep its counsel on its exact position ahead of the meeting starting in Vienna on June 25.
OPEC President, Libyan Oil Minister Abdallah al-Badri, said last month he expected the group to maintain quotas unchanged under its official output ceiling of 25.03 million barrels a day (bpd).
Actual production is running closer to 27 million bpd, underlining the group's increasing failure in recent years to act as a true commodity cartel.
The slump in world oil prices over recent weeks has refocused attention on the rampant violations of mandated OPEC quotas.
International benchmark North Sea Brent blend has slumped to $17.50, down more than 40 percent from just short of $25 in January.
"I think there will be some stress on the need to adhere to quotas," said the Gulf source.
The slide in prices has threatened to put renewed pressure on oil exporting countries' budgets after last year's unexpected windfalls when crude hit six-year highs.
While a handful of Gulf producers led by Saudi Arabia maintain spare capacity and output discipline, others like Venezuela and Nigeria are pumping at full steam without regard for oil prices.
Others like Iran and Libya have not strayed beyond official limitations but have little choice because of capacity constraints.
Iran's Gholamreza Aghazadeh is likely to take the lead in any fresh attempt to corral OPEC's overzealous producers.
Aghazadeh in May drew fresh vows to stick to quota from an informal meeting in Isfahan, Iran, of seven OPEC member countries.
The Iranian minister will chair a regular session of OPEC's quota compliance committee on June 24, the day before full ministerial talks begin.
But observers dismiss any real hope of the quota violators, buoyed by foreign oil company investors, reining in output.
"Zero chance," said one OPEC national oil company executive.
